CausalChain: Obesity and/or NAFLD lead to elevated circulating FFAs -> In HCC, reduced DGAT2 activity causes decreased conversion of FFAs into triglycerides -> Accumulated FFAs increase lipotoxic stress and activate oncogenic signaling pathways -> This promotes dedifferentiation, proliferation, and metastasis of HCC cells -> Enhancing DGAT2 restores TG production, enabling formation of protective lipid droplets -> Sequestration of FFAs reduces lipotoxicity and oncogenic signaling -> This results in decreased tumor progression.
Hypothesis: Enhancement of DGAT2 activity in hepatocellular carcinoma will promote the formation of protective lipid droplets that sequester lipotoxic free fatty acids, thereby reducing oncogenic signaling and tumor aggressiveness, ultimately improving patient outcomes.
Abstract: Emerging evidence from lipidomic studies in liver cancer suggests that dysregulated triglyceride synthesis may be an intrinsic contributor to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression. In particular, reduced activity or expression of diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2) in HCC cells appears to correlate with a dedifferentiated, aggressive phenotype, potentially due to the accumulation of free fatty acids (FFAs) that can induce lipotoxicity and activate oncogenic signaling pathways. We propose that re‐activation or enhancement of DGAT2 activity in HCC cells may drive the re‐formation of lipid droplets that sequester lipotoxic FFAs, thereby mitigating cellular stress and attenuating oncogenic processes. Targeted upregulation of DGAT2 might restore a metabolic balance within tumor cells, promoting a more differentiated state and reducing tumor aggressiveness. This hypothesis paves the way for potential lipid‐modulating strategies as part of HCC therapeutics.
